summary.title: Producing wrong data without doing anything obviously wrong! (ASPLOS'09)
summary.one_liner: Small, seemingly innocuous details of an experimental setup, such as link order and environment size, can bias systems measurements enough to lead researchers to wrong conclusions.
keywords: how to avoid misleading benchmark results
takeaways: Seemingly innocuous setup details (e.g., link order, environment size) can introduce measurement bias that flips a comparison between S and S+I.
The authors found measurement bias in all architectures, compilers, and SPEC CPU2006 C programs they tested.
A survey of 133 papers from ASPLOS, PACT, PLDI, and CGO found none adequately considered measurement bias.
Two methods are proposed: causal analysis to detect bias and setup randomization to avoid it.
summary.summary: This ASPLOS'09 paper by Mytkowicz, Diwan, Hauswirth, and Sweeney argues that changing an apparently minor aspect of an experiment can lead systems researchers to draw wrong conclusions about whether an idea helps a system. The authors show measurement bias is significant (it can change conclusions) and common, across Pentium 4, Core 2, and m5 O3CPU, gcc and Intel's C compiler, and all SPEC CPU2006 C programs. A literature survey of 133 recent papers found none adequately addressed it. They describe and demonstrate two remedies borrowed from other sciences: causal analysis to detect bias and setup randomization to avoid it. The page is an abstract with BibTeX citation rather than the full text.
